questions.q: John Stuart Mill's harm principle, as developed in his utilitarian framework, holds that restricting an individual's freedom is only justified when:
options: The action violates a universal moral rule that all persons should follow
The action conflicts with the professional standards of the relevant industry
The action causes harm to others, not merely because it is offensive or distasteful to society
The action fails to produce a measurable benefit for the person performing it
questions.note: Mill's harm principle, articulated in 'On Liberty' (1859), states that the only legitimate reason to exercise power over another person against their will is to prevent harm to others. Mere offense or self-harm does not meet the threshold. This is a core utilitarian limit on collective power.

explain.correct: Mill's harm principle permits restricting freedom only to prevent harm to others — not for offense, distaste, or the actor's own good.
wrong: Acting on a universal moral rule is Kant's deontological test, not Mill's harm principle.
Industry professional standards are external codes, not the utilitarian harm test.
Utilitarian analysis focuses on effects on all persons affected, not just the actor's own benefit.

questions.q: W.D. Ross's theory of prima facie duties differs from Kant's categorical imperative most significantly because Ross argues that:
options: Moral duties can conflict, and a reasonable person must weigh them against each other in context
An action is ethical only if it can be universalized as a law for all rational agents without contradiction
The consequences of an action for the greatest number of people determine its moral worth
Virtue and character are the foundation of ethical behavior, not abstract rules
questions.note: W.D. Ross (1930) proposed prima facie duties — obligations such as fidelity, non-maleficence, and beneficence — that are genuinely binding but can be overridden when they conflict. Unlike Kant's absolute universal law, Ross holds that context determines which duty is stronger in a given situation.

explain.correct: Ross's key departure from Kant is that duties can conflict and must be weighed contextually — none is automatically absolute.
wrong: Universalizing a maxim without contradiction is Kant's categorical imperative, not Ross's theory.
Consequences for the greatest number is the utilitarian standard, not Ross's duty-based framework.
Grounding ethics in virtue and character describes Aristotle's virtue ethics, not Ross.

questions.q: In the 1990s, tobacco companies publicly denied internal research showing nicotine addiction while their lawyers confirmed the research remained private and undisclosed to regulators. This conduct was largely legal at the time but ethically condemned because:
options: The companies were required by federal law to share all internal research with the public
Their internal research was inaccurate and therefore had no legal standing
Deliberately withholding known health harms from the public violates the ethical duty of honesty even when no specific disclosure law existed
The executives had personal obligations under the ACM Code of Ethics to disclose safety data
questions.note: Tobacco litigation documents revealed that companies possessed internal proof of addiction decades before public disclosure. No law at the time compelled proactive disclosure of private research. The ethical failure was the deliberate suppression of known harms — a breach of honesty and respect for persons regardless of legality.

explain.correct: Deliberately suppressing known health harms violates the ethical duty of honesty and respect for persons even when no specific disclosure law requires it.
wrong: No federal law at the time required public sharing of private internal research.
Accuracy of the research is irrelevant to the ethical and legal analysis of suppression.
The ACM Code applies to computing professionals, not tobacco executives.

questions.q: The IEEE Code of Ethics, like the ACM Code, places engineers' obligations to public safety above obligations to employers. An electrical engineer who discovers a safety defect in a shipped product and is instructed by management to stay silent is ethically obligated to:
options: Stay silent, because the engineer's employment contract supersedes the code
Accept management's judgment, because product liability rests with the company, not individual engineers
Raise the safety concern internally and, if management fails to act, report it to the appropriate regulatory or safety body
Wait for a user to be harmed before reporting, to ensure the defect is confirmed real-world
questions.note: The IEEE Code of Ethics requires engineers to hold public safety, health, and welfare paramount. When internal escalation fails, external reporting to a regulatory or safety authority is the ethical obligation. Waiting for injury is a dereliction of professional duty.

explain.correct: IEEE's Code requires engineers to put public safety first — raise internally, and if unresolved, report to the appropriate regulatory body.
wrong: Employment contracts cannot override a professional code that places public safety above employer loyalty.
Product liability resting with the company does not relieve the individual engineer of the ethical duty to act.
Waiting for a confirmed injury to occur before reporting is a clear dereliction of the duty to protect public safety.

questions.q: The EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) Article 7 requires that consent to data processing must be 'freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous.' A cookie banner that is pre-ticked to 'accept all' and requires users to navigate three sub-menus to decline tracking fails this standard primarily because:
options: The banner is displayed in a language the user may not understand
Pre-ticked boxes and friction-laden opt-outs do not constitute freely given, unambiguous consent
Cookies are categorically excluded from the GDPR consent framework
GDPR consent only applies to sensitive categories of data such as health or biometric data
questions.note: GDPR Recital 32 explicitly states that pre-ticked boxes do not constitute valid consent. GDPR Article 7(3) and guidance from the European Data Protection Board confirm that designing opt-out as significantly harder than opt-in (a 'dark pattern') negates the 'freely given' and 'unambiguous' requirements.

explain.correct: Pre-ticked boxes and friction-laden opt-outs are GDPR dark patterns that fail the 'freely given' and 'unambiguous' consent requirements.
wrong: Language accessibility is a separate concern; the core failure here is the dark pattern design, not translation.
Cookies — especially tracking cookies — are squarely within the GDPR consent framework.
GDPR consent obligations apply to all personal data processing, not only sensitive categories.

questions.q: In the Theranos scandal, software and lab engineers developed systems they knew produced inaccurate blood-test results that were reported to patients as accurate. From a deontological perspective, the engineers' participation was unethical primarily because:
options: The company ultimately failed financially, proving the business model was unsound
The engineers received compensation for work that harmed the company's investors
Knowingly producing false medical results deceives patients in a way that violates their dignity and autonomy as ends in themselves
The engineers should have calculated the probability that patients would act on incorrect results before deciding to participate
questions.note: Kantian deontology holds that persons must be treated as ends in themselves, never merely as means. Patients who receive fabricated diagnostic results are being used as instruments of corporate fraud — their autonomy and ability to make real medical decisions are violated regardless of whether anyone was harmed in a particular instance.

explain.correct: From a Kantian view, producing false medical results treats patients as means to corporate ends rather than as autonomous persons — wrong in itself.
wrong: Financial failure is an outcome; deontology judges the act itself, not its results.
Harm to investors is relevant to legal claims but is not the central deontological wrong here.
Calculating harm probabilities before acting is a consequentialist approach, not a deontological one.

questions.q: Alasdair MacIntyre, in 'After Virtue' (1981), argues that modern moral philosophy has lost its way because it abandoned which Aristotelian concept essential for understanding human ethics?
options: The categorical imperative, which grounds morality in universal reason
The utilitarian calculus, which grounds morality in measurable social welfare
The concept of telos — a purpose or end toward which a human life and its practices are directed
The social contract, which grounds morality in the agreement of rational agents
questions.note: MacIntyre's 'After Virtue' argues that Enlightenment moral philosophy discarded Aristotle's concept of telos (human purpose/end), leaving moral claims as mere expressions of preference. Recovering telos — the idea that humans and their practices have characteristic ends — is, for MacIntyre, essential to coherent ethics.

explain.correct: MacIntyre argues modern ethics lost coherence by abandoning Aristotle's concept of telos — the purpose or end that gives human action its moral direction.
wrong: The categorical imperative is Kant's, not Aristotle's, and MacIntyre critiques Kantian deontology as part of the problem.
Utilitarian calculus is precisely one of the Enlightenment frameworks MacIntyre criticizes for lacking telos.
The social contract is associated with Locke, Rousseau, and Rawls — not Aristotle's virtue ethics.

questions.q: A healthcare software company builds a telehealth platform that processes patient appointment notes and billing codes. They contract with a cloud-based AI service to auto-summarize clinical notes. Under HIPAA, before the AI service may process any patient data, the healthcare company must:
options: Obtain each patient's written authorization to share their notes with the AI vendor
Register the AI vendor with the Department of Health and Human Services
Ensure all data sent to the AI service is anonymized using de-identification methods specified in 45 CFR 164.514
Execute a Business Associate Agreement with the AI vendor that binds it to HIPAA's administrative, physical, and technical safeguard requirements
questions.note: Under HIPAA's Business Associate provisions (45 CFR 164.502(e) and 164.504(e)), a covered entity must have a signed Business Associate Agreement (BAA) before sharing PHI with any vendor that performs functions on its behalf. The BAA contractually obligates the vendor to implement the same safeguards as the covered entity.

explain.correct: A signed Business Associate Agreement binding the AI vendor to HIPAA safeguards is required before any PHI is shared with it.
wrong: Patient authorization is not required for treatment-related operations performed by business associates under a valid BAA.
HHS does not maintain a registry of business associates; the BAA is the required instrument.

De-identification under 45 CFR 164.514 removes HIPAA applicability, but if the company wants the AI to process real PHI (e.g., accurate clinical notes), de-identification defeats the purpose — the BAA is the correct path.

questions.q: Under the GDPR Article 33, when an organization discovers a personal data breach that is likely to result in risk to individuals' rights and freedoms, it must notify the relevant supervisory authority within:
options: 30 days of discovering the breach
72 hours of becoming aware of the breach
As soon as it has completed a full internal forensic investigation
Only if the number of affected individuals exceeds 500
questions.note: GDPR Article 33 sets a 72-hour notification window to the competent supervisory authority from the moment the controller becomes 'aware' of a breach likely to pose risk. If the full picture is not yet known, an initial notification must still be submitted and supplemented later. There is no minimum threshold of affected individuals.

explain.correct: GDPR Article 33 requires supervisory authority notification within 72 hours of becoming aware of a breach likely to risk individuals' rights.
wrong: The GDPR deadline is 72 hours, not 30 days; many US state breach laws use 30 or 45 days, but GDPR does not.
Waiting for a complete forensic investigation before notifying violates the 72-hour rule; partial information can be notified with supplements to follow.
GDPR has no minimum threshold of affected persons for the Article 33 supervisory notification obligation.

questions.q: A private university in the United States bans a student organization from using campus social media accounts to post political content, citing a content-neutral policy against partisan speech on official university channels. A student argues this violates the First Amendment. The student's claim is:
options: Valid, because universities are educational institutions and political speech is the most protected form
Valid, because any policy limiting speech based on viewpoint or subject matter is per se unconstitutional
Likely weak if the university is private, because the First Amendment restrains government actors, not private institutions
Valid, because the university receives federal funding through student financial aid, making it a state actor for all speech purposes
questions.note: The First Amendment protects individuals from government censorship. Private universities, unlike public universities (which are state actors), are generally not bound by the First Amendment in their speech policies. Federal funding does not by itself convert a private institution into a state actor for First Amendment purposes.

explain.correct: Private universities are not government actors; the First Amendment does not bind them, making the student's claim likely weak.
wrong: Political speech being 'most protected' applies to government restrictions, not private institutional policies.
Viewpoint and subject-matter discrimination analysis applies to government restrictions, not private actors.
Federal funding (e.g., through Title IV financial aid) does not automatically make a private institution a First Amendment state actor — courts have consistently held otherwise.

questions.q: A YouTube content creator records a 10-minute video reviewing a newly released film. The video includes 45 seconds of unedited footage from the film to illustrate points made in the critique. Under the four-factor fair use analysis (17 U.S.C. § 107), which factor MOST strongly favors the creator?
options: The effect of the use on the potential market for the original film
The amount and substantiality of the portion used relative to the whole work
The purpose and character of the use -- specifically that it is transformative commentary and criticism
The nature of the copyrighted work -- a creative fictional film
questions.note: Courts applying fair use consistently identify the first factor — purpose and character of use — as most significant, with transformative use (commentary, criticism, parody) being the strongest indicator. Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music (1994) established that a commercial purpose does not defeat fair use when the work is genuinely transformative.

explain.correct: Transformative commentary and criticism under the purpose-and-character factor most strongly favors the creator in a film review use case.
wrong: Market effect (factor 4) is also important but typically weighs against the user when the use substitutes for the original; here, a review is unlikely to substitute for the film itself.
Amount used (factor 3) weighs against the creator since 45 seconds of unedited footage may be substantial in quality even if small in quantity.
Nature of the work (factor 2) disfavors fair use for creative fictional works, as they receive strong copyright protection.

questions.q: A startup uses a library licensed under the GNU Lesser General Public License (LGPL v2.1) by dynamically linking it into their proprietary application. They distribute the application without releasing its source code. Under the LGPL, this arrangement:
options: Violates the license, because any software that links to an LGPL library must release all source code under the GPL
Is generally permitted, because the LGPL was specifically designed to allow dynamic linking from proprietary software without triggering copyleft on the larger work
Requires the startup to pay a royalty to the Free Software Foundation for commercial use
Requires the startup to publish the application's source code within 12 months of distribution
questions.note: The LGPL was created precisely to allow libraries to be used by proprietary applications through dynamic linking, without requiring the entire application to be released as open source. The startup must still make the LGPL library's own source available and allow users to re-link with a modified library version, but the proprietary application code itself is not subject to copyleft.

explain.correct: The LGPL permits dynamic linking from proprietary software; the copyleft obligation extends to modifications of the library itself, not to the larger application.
wrong: LGPL was specifically designed to avoid this outcome — dynamic linking from proprietary software is its primary allowed use case, unlike the full GPL.
The LGPL is a free software license; it charges no royalties, whether for commercial or non-commercial use.
There is no 12-month grace period in the LGPL; the 'generally permitted' answer covers this scenario.

questions.q: A fitness app collects users' heart rate, sleep patterns, and GPS routes, and shares this data with health insurance underwriters under a generic clause buried in its terms of service stating data may be shared with 'business partners.' Which privacy principle is most directly violated?
options: Data minimization, because the app collects more data types than are needed for fitness tracking
Data accuracy, because the app cannot guarantee the accuracy of biometric readings shared with insurers
Transparency and notice, because users are not clearly informed that biometric data will be shared with insurers who may use it to affect coverage decisions
Storage limitation, because the data is retained longer than needed to provide the fitness service
questions.note: Sharing sensitive biometric data with insurance underwriters under vague 'business partners' language is a paradigmatic transparency and notice failure. Users cannot make informed decisions about a product if its most consequential data uses — ones with real-life financial and health implications — are obscured in legalese.

explain.correct: Sharing biometric data with insurance underwriters under vague terms, without clear notice, most directly violates the transparency and notice principle.
wrong: Data minimization concerns the volume of categories collected for the stated purpose; the core failure here is undisclosed sharing, not over-collection.
Data accuracy concerns whether records are correct, not how they are disclosed or shared.
Storage limitation concerns how long data is retained; the primary violation here is the undisclosed sharing, not the retention period.

questions.q: China's Social Credit System assigns citizens aggregate behavioral scores based on financial history, online activity, social associations, and public behavior, with low scores triggering travel bans and restricted access to services. The most central ethical concern about this system is:
options: The risk of data breaches exposing citizens' score histories to foreign governments
The computational cost of aggregating behavioral data at national scale
Pervasive scoring and punishment for lawful behavior produces a chilling effect on personal autonomy, freedom of association, and dissent
The system's lack of technical transparency about the algorithm used to calculate scores
questions.note: The Social Credit System's central ethical problem — discussed extensively in surveillance scholarship and human rights reporting — is that it extends state power into every domain of private life and punishes behavior that may be entirely legal, creating incentives to conform and self-censor. This chilling effect on autonomy and dissent is the core ethical indictment, not the system's data security or algorithmic opacity.

explain.correct: The core ethical concern is that pervasive behavioral scoring chills personal autonomy, free association, and lawful dissent — extending state power into all aspects of daily life.
wrong: Foreign breach risk is a security concern, secondary to the fundamental civil-liberties violation.
Computational cost is an engineering concern with no bearing on the ethical core of the system.
Algorithmic opacity is a fairness concern but is not the primary ethical objection — the system's chilling effect on freedom is.

questions.q: In 2014, the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs discovered that its scheduling software was allowing staff to manipulate appointment wait-time data, concealing dangerous delays in veteran care. A software analyst who discovered the manipulation and reported it internally but was ignored would be ethically obligated, under professional codes of conduct, to:
options: Continue documenting the manipulation internally while awaiting management action indefinitely
Accept management's inaction because the harm was indirect — caused by staff using the software, not the software itself
Escalate to external oversight, such as the VA Inspector General or Congress, because the internal channel failed and patient safety was at stake
Perform an unauthorized fix to the scheduling software to close the manipulation vector
questions.note: When internal escalation fails and the harm is serious — in this case, veterans dying due to concealed wait times — professional codes (ACM, IEEE) support escalating to external oversight bodies. The VA wait-time scandal resulted in Congressional hearings and an Inspector General investigation after internal whistleblowers were ignored.

explain.correct: When internal escalation fails and patient safety is at stake, professional codes support escalating to external oversight bodies such as an Inspector General or relevant legislative body.
wrong: Waiting indefinitely after internal channels have failed leaves ongoing harm unaddressed — inaction is not ethically neutral.
Harm being indirect (staff using broken software) does not discharge the analyst's professional duty when the harm is foreseeable and serious.
Performing an unauthorized modification to a government system raises its own serious legal and ethical problems, and is not what professional codes recommend.

questions.q: Reuters revealed in 2018 that Amazon had scrapped an experimental AI recruiting tool after discovering it systematically down-ranked resumes from women. The tool had been trained on 10 years of past hiring decisions made predominantly by male hiring managers. This case illustrates which core AI ethics concept?
options: A model trained on biased historical data will encode and perpetuate those historical biases, producing disparate impact against protected groups
Proprietary AI models are too opaque for even their creators to audit for bias
AI recruiting tools are always illegal under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act when disparate impact is detected
The model's failure demonstrates that neural networks cannot reliably process unstructured text such as resumes
questions.note: Amazon's recruiting tool is a canonical case study in training-data bias. Because the training data reflected historical hiring patterns skewed toward men, the model learned to prefer patterns associated with male candidates — penalizing resumes that included words like 'women's' (as in women's chess club). The case demonstrates how historical bias is amplified, not merely replicated, by ML systems.

explain.correct: The Amazon case illustrates that models trained on historically biased data encode and amplify those biases, producing disparate impact against underrepresented groups.
wrong: Amazon was able to audit the model and discover the bias — opacity is not the central lesson here.

Disparate impact does not automatically make an AI tool illegal; legality depends on whether it was deployed in employment decisions and whether the disparity meets legal thresholds — Amazon stopped the tool before deployment in production hiring.
The model's ability to process text was not the failure; the failure was the biased training corpus, not the architecture.

questions.q: The FCC's 2021 Affordable Connectivity Program (ACP) was created to subsidize broadband access for low-income households. The social problem it addresses is best characterized as:
options: The growing cybersecurity risk posed by unsecured home networks in low-income neighborhoods
The inadequacy of existing telecommunications infrastructure to support 5G deployment in urban areas
Unequal access to broadband connectivity that disadvantages low-income households in education, employment, healthcare, and civic participation
The inability of legacy DSL technology to meet minimum bandwidth requirements for streaming services
questions.note: The Affordable Connectivity Program directly targets the digital divide — the gap in broadband access and affordability across socioeconomic lines. When schooling, telehealth, remote work, and government services move online, lack of affordable home broadband translates directly into educational and economic disadvantage.

explain.correct: The ACP addresses the digital divide: unequal broadband access that disadvantages low-income households across education, employment, healthcare, and civic life.
wrong: Cybersecurity risk in home networks is a separate concern unrelated to the access-subsidy purpose of the ACP.
5G urban deployment is an infrastructure expansion initiative, not a low-income access equity program.
DSL obsolescence is a technology-upgrade issue, not the access-equity problem the ACP was designed to solve.

questions.q: A mobile banking app requests permission to access the user's device microphone at install time, justifying it as needed for future voice-command features not yet built. The most ethical design approach, consistent with the principle of data minimization, is:
options: Request microphone permission at install time with a clear explanation of the planned future feature
Request microphone permission only at the time the voice-command feature is actually built, enabled, and actively used by the user
Add a settings toggle that allows users to revoke microphone access after granting it
Disclose the microphone access in the app's privacy policy and proceed with the install-time request
questions.note: Data minimization requires that access to personal data — including sensor access — be limited to what is necessary for a current, specific purpose. Requesting microphone access for a feature that does not yet exist fails this principle: there is no current legitimate purpose, and the permission collects capability far beyond present need. Just-in-time permission requests, triggered when the feature is actually used, are the privacy-by-design standard.

explain.correct: Data minimization requires requesting microphone access only when the voice-command feature is actually built and in use — not speculatively at install time.
wrong: Explaining the planned future feature at install time is more transparent but still fails data minimization — there is no current purpose justifying the access.
A revocation toggle improves user control but doesn't fix the initial over-collection; granting access before it's needed is still a minimization failure.
Disclosing the access in a privacy policy makes it transparent but does not satisfy the proportionality requirement of data minimization.

questions.q: In 2014, Facebook conducted a psychological experiment on approximately 689,000 users by secretly manipulating the emotional content of their News Feeds to study contagion of mood. Users were not informed or asked to consent specifically to the experiment. The core ethical violation was:
options: Facebook lacked the technical infrastructure to implement the study at scale without performance degradation
The study violated IRB (Institutional Review Board) norms requiring informed consent before using human subjects in research, even when a general terms-of-service agreement existed
The results of the study were published without peer review, violating academic publishing standards
Facebook's data scientists were not licensed psychologists and were therefore unqualified to conduct behavioral research
questions.note: The 2014 Facebook emotional contagion study sparked significant ethical controversy. The core objection was that human subjects research — even by private companies — has traditionally required informed consent under norms derived from the Belmont Report and enforced by IRBs. A general terms-of-service clause was not considered adequate substitute for specific informed consent to experimental manipulation.

explain.correct: The core violation was using human subjects in behavioral research without specific informed consent, contrary to IRB norms derived from the Belmont Report.
wrong: Technical infrastructure was not a factor; Facebook deployed the study successfully — the problem was ethical, not operational.
Publication venue is a separate academic concern; the core ethical failure preceded publication.
Licensing credentials for data scientists is not the issue; the consent requirement applies regardless of the researcher's professional background.

questions.q: Langdon Winner's influential 1980 essay 'Do Artifacts Have Politics?' argues that technology is not neutral by using the example of Robert Moses' low bridges on Long Island parkways, which were allegedly designed too low for public buses. The broader principle Winner establishes is:
options: Public infrastructure projects should require congressional approval before construction
Design decisions embed political and social values — technology shapes who can participate, who is excluded, and who holds power
Transportation systems are inherently more political than digital technologies and should be regulated differently
Engineers must obtain public consent before building infrastructure that affects low-income communities
questions.note: Winner's essay is a foundational text in Science and Technology Studies and technoethics. His central argument is that artifacts embody politics: the design of a physical or digital system can encode values, enforce hierarchies, and distribute power — often invisibly. The Moses bridge example (disputed by some historians, but analytically valuable) illustrates how design choices exclude certain users without ever naming them in policy.

explain.correct: Winner's argument is that design choices embed political and social values — determining who participates, who is excluded, and how power is distributed.
wrong: Congressional approval is a governance mechanism unrelated to Winner's philosophical argument about design and politics.
Winner's argument applies explicitly to digital and information technologies, not only transportation; the essay directly influenced computing ethics scholarship.
Requiring public consent is a policy prescription Winner does not advance; his argument is analytical — artifacts already have politics, whether designers acknowledge it or not.
